touches.text: Device: its own process, in the rack, on the bus. See 2.
DEVICE (Implemented as BaseDevice, part of the base tool; a first class object)
COMMANDS:

Any device or machine may have a bin/ beside its code (cairn/devices/<device>/bin/, .../machines/<machine>/bin/). That folder IS its list of shortcuts: add a file to add one, delete it to remove one. A shortcut is just a script that calls the long form, which also saves the walk from searching farther (eg `cairn superclaude` → `cairn cc superclaude`; `cairn show temp` → `cairn recovery show temp`), or does work itself (eg initialization, install). Shortcuts can go anywhere, beside what they serve (RULE 1).
`cairn foo` whose first word is not a device means `cairn cairn foo`: top-level shortcuts are the cairn device's bin/.
OPERATOR DEVICE (cairn/devices/operator/)
PURPOSE: This device represents the operator(s) of the system
INTENTION:
This device represents the user on the bus
This device's web panel is the operator's to do list...
Email
Trouble Tickets
Open questions (the ones only the operator can answer)
The list is live: items appear as they arrive and leave as they're answered or resolved.

Artifacts awaiting review are not on the operator's to-do list. The artifact review process is replaced: the intentions say what it should look like, and CC assesses each artifact against them, one of:
Machine: the operator inbox (today the operator_inbox tool, 19.17) builds the to-do list from live state, storing nothing.

More than one operator means instances: operator 0 is Akien, operator 1 someone else. CC never acts as an operator; it always speaks as the CC device, so it can never accept an ask that only an operator may (eg a root ask, 7.3.9.4). (Q#26, Akien 2026-11-04: "agreed on all counts")
WHY:
COMMANDS:
The `cairn` command is the operator's interface into the system, so it is special: it speaks as the operator (8.2.3), and most of it is shortcuts, which are shell scripts. (Akien, 2026-11-05)

Two execution trees: at each segment, if there is a script for it in that device's bin, run it; otherwise go onto the bus and ask that device. Why: scripts are the simple path, and the bus is the operator's route to what a device answers itself, often faster (eg `cairn codemother show artifact <id>`). (Akien, 2026-11-05)

`cairn help` lists [all], then [operator], then [cairn], then every other device in alphabetical order, because `cairn` itself is special. Help is called, returns its results, and is done. Help at any other level looks in the bin folders inside that device's tree for the shortcuts relevant to the input. (Akien, 2026-11-05)
Answering a question is the operator acting, so it is `cairn operator answer <id> "<words>"` (a script if there is one, else the bus), never a verb on whichever device asked. (Q#27, Akien 2026-11-05)
operator_inbox: builds the operator's to-do list from live state. → Operator's machine (8.2.7)
question: the open-question door: a decision only you can make, bound to its ticket, answered in your words. → Ticket (3.3.5)? Operator?
